what: Citations link each sentence of an AI answer back to the exact passage it came from, so a reader (or a checker) can see where every claim was grounded.
like: Like footnotes in a school essay: each fact points to the page in the book where you read it, so the teacher can check.
why: Users can verify the answer instead of trusting it blindly
Makes hallucinations visible and measurable, sentence by sentence
Sends credit and clicks back to the sources - the heart of AI search visibility

steps.d: The best passages from retrieval and reranking go into the prompt, each with an id, title and URL, so the model has something concrete to point at.
Passages are chunked into sentences (or your own blocks). That chunk size is the finest thing a citation can point to - a passage-level citation.
The model writes the answer and tags each claim with the chunk ids it used. Provider features return these as structured fields, not loose [1] text.
The parser links each answer span to a source location - a character range, page range or block range - plus the exact quoted text for the footnote.
A support checker asks: does the cited text actually entail this sentence? An NLI model (natural language inference) or an LLM judge says yes or no.
Scores roll up into citation precision and recall. Unsupported sentences are removed, rewritten, or sent back for another pass before the user sees them.

numbers.l: of ELI5 answers lacked full citation support, even best models
max citations per statement in ALCE - more rarely helped
cited_text in Claude citations does not count as output tokens
Claude citation locations: character, page and content block ranges

choices.d: Sentence chunks give precise footnotes; custom blocks (bullets, transcript lines) give you control. Too coarse and a citation proves little; too fine and answers fill up with markers.

Use the provider feature where you can: Claude citations return guaranteed-valid pointers into your documents, OpenAI web search returns url_citation annotations with start and end indexes in the text.
A small NLI model is cheap and fast for every sentence; an LLM judge handles paraphrase and multi-source claims better. Many teams run NLI online and a judge offline.
Drop the sentence, soften it, regenerate with stricter instructions, or show it without a citation and a lower-confidence style. Pick per product risk.
Answer engines show a handful of sources, not every passage read. Cap citations per claim and prefer the most specific, most trusted source.

instead.why: Grades groundedness after the fact instead of per sentence inline
Blocks unsafe or ungrounded output without showing sources
Better evidence in the prompt means fewer weak citations to clean up
Track citation precision and recall over a fixed test set

breaks.d: The model cites a source id or URL that was never in the context.
breaks.see: Footnotes that 404 or ids outside the passage list
breaks.fix: Use native citation APIs or validate every id against the context before rendering

breaks.d: The link exists but the passage does not say what the sentence says.
breaks.see: Low citation recall from the NLI or judge check
breaks.fix: Check entailment per sentence; drop or rewrite unsupported claims

breaks.d: Extra sources are attached that add nothing.
breaks.see: Low citation precision; many sources per sentence
breaks.fix: Cap citations per claim and score each one for its own support

breaks.d: The model answers from training data and adds no citation.
breaks.see: Sentences with zero citations in grounded mode
breaks.fix: Instruct to answer only from sources, and flag uncited sentences

breaks.d: Scanned PDFs or images have no text to point at.
breaks.fix: Run OCR first, or pass text as custom content blocks

say: I'll put the reranked passages into the prompt as numbered documents and use the provider's citation feature, so every claim comes back with a pointer to an exact span.
Before showing the answer, a support check asks whether each cited passage actually entails its sentence, using a small NLI model online and an LLM judge offline.
I'll track citation recall - are claims backed - and citation precision - does each citation help - next to answer quality in our eval set.
For answer engines, the pages that get cited tend to be the ones with clear, self-contained factual sentences that are easy to quote.

followups.q: How do you measure citation quality?
followups.a: Citation recall: share of statements fully supported by their cited passages. Citation precision: share of citations that actually help support their statement. Both use an entailment check, as in the ALCE benchmark, alongside answer correctness.

followups.q: Why not just ask the model to write [1] in its text?
followups.a: It works, but ids can be invented and quotes cost output tokens. Native features parse citations into structured fields: Claude guarantees valid pointers to supplied documents, and cited_text is not billed as output.

followups.q: Why do some pages get cited by AI answer engines and others not?
followups.a: Engines retrieve, rerank, then quote passages that directly support a sentence. Pages with clear, specific, self-contained factual statements are easy to extract and entail, so they win the few citation slots.

followups.q: Can you combine citations with JSON output?
followups.a: Not on Claude today: citations interleave citation blocks with text, so enabling them together with structured outputs returns a 400 error. Ask for citations first, then convert in a second step.

today: Claude's citations feature is generally available on all active models and returns character, page or content block locations, while OpenAI's web search returns url_citation annotations with title, URL and text span.

check.q: A sentence has a citation, but the passage does not say that. Which metric drops?
check.why: Recall asks whether each statement is fully supported by what it cites.

check.q: What usually checks if a passage supports a sentence?
check.a: An entailment (NLI) model or LLM judge
check.why: Support is about meaning: does the passage logically back the claim?

check.q: In Claude's citations, how is a plain text location given?
check.why: Plain text uses char indexes; PDFs use 1-indexed page ranges.

check.q: Why do native citation APIs beat prompt-only [1] markers?
check.a: Pointers are parsed and always valid
d: They remove the need for retrieval
check.why: The API extracts cited text from your documents, so ids cannot be invented.
